text: Every grain of sand here is five thousand people. Whenever more people die than normal, their grains are lifted away.
In the second century, plague crosses the Roman Empire, and Han China falls into civil war.
In 541, bubonic plague reaches Constantinople: the first great plague pandemic.
In 755, the An Lushan rebellion tears Tang China apart.
From 1211, the Mongol conquests. Cities from northern China to Persia are emptied.
In 1346, the Black Death reaches the Black Sea. In seven years it kills between a third and a half of Europe.
After Columbus, smallpox and other new diseases reach the Americas. Within a century, nine in ten of their people are gone.
In the sixteen hundreds, the Thirty Years' War in Germany, and the fall of the Ming in China.
For three and a half centuries, the Atlantic slave trade kills millions of Africans, in capture and on the crossing.
In 1770, a great famine strikes Bengal, under East India Company rule.
In 1812, Napoleon marches into Russia. Most of his army never comes home.
In 1817, cholera spreads out of Bengal, and returns to India for a century.
In 1851, the Taiping Rebellion: a civil war in southern China that kills some twenty million people.
In 1876, drought brings famine to India and northern China. Nearly twenty million die.
In King Leopold's Congo, forced labour, violence and disease kill millions.
In 1896, plague reaches Bombay. Over thirty years it kills about ten million in India.
In 1914, the First World War. Soldiers' grains leave their homes for the fronts where they died.
In 1918, influenza: twenty-five million dead in two years, nearly half of them in India.
In Russia, civil war, and then famine on the Volga.
In 1932, Stalin's collectivisation brings famine to Ukraine and Kazakhstan.
In 1937, Japan invades China.
In 1941, Germany invades the Soviet Union, and the Holocaust begins. Six million Jews will be murdered.
Stalingrad. In seven months, some seven hundred thousand soldiers and civilians die.
War brings famine to Bengal. By 1945, the war has killed nearly seventy million people.
From 1950, the United Nations counts every country's deaths, every year.
In 1959, Mao's Great Leap Forward: the deadliest famine in history. Fifteen to forty-five million die.
In the 1990s, AIDS spreads across southern and eastern Africa.
In 2020, COVID-19: from Wuhan to Lombardy, New York, and India's Delta wave. Twenty-six million deaths above normal.
Six hundred and forty million people, lifted away. And before 1950, only the catastrophes large enough to be counted.
